title: The Gang of Four and 'Design Patterns' (1994)
explainer: The 23 patterns in this lesson come from one 1994 book, 'Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software,' written by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, and John Vlissides - a group cited together so often that the field just calls them 'the Gang of Four.' The book didn't invent most of the techniques it describes; it catalogued and named recurring solutions the authors had already seen working programmers reach for, which is part of why the vocabulary stuck so widely. It has sold more than half a million copies and remains the shared reference point most later object-oriented design writing talks back to.

title: Christopher Alexander's Architectural Patterns, Borrowed for Software (1977/1987)
explainer: The idea of a 'pattern' as a named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem didn't start in software - it came from architect Christopher Alexander's 1977 book 'A Pattern Language: Towns, Buildings, Construction,' which catalogued solutions for designing livable buildings and towns. In 1987, programmers Kent Beck and Ward Cunningham presented Alexander's pattern-language idea at the OOPSLA conference as a way to describe object-oriented user-interface designs, and that cross-disciplinary borrowing is what the Gang of Four built on seven years later. It's a useful reminder that 'patterns,' as a way of capturing design wisdom, were never inherently specific to code.
